title: The unwholesome four
hookLine: delusion, shamelessness, recklessness, restlessness: present in every unwholesome moment

lines: THE GAPS SHOW IN THE RAIN.
cards: "As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind." That's a verse from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation.
A roof with gaps doesn't look like trouble on a dry afternoon. It shows itself when the weather turns, one drip at a time, right over the bed.
Today the Abhidhamma points at the gaps: four factors it finds in every unwholesome moment of mind, whatever else is going on in it.

teach.b: First, the word. Unwholesome translates akusala, the opposite of kusala, skillful or healthy. It's not a verdict on a person.

In the suttas, the Buddha tells his son Rahula to look at an action before, during and after it, and to ask one thing: does this lead to harm, for me, for others, or for both? A state that leads to harm is unskillful.
That's the test, not a label. Now the four. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha says that whenever a moment is unwholesome, these are present.
Delusion, moha: the mind can't see clearly what it's doing, like walking in fog. Shamelessness, ahirika: no inner pull of, this isn't who I want to be.

teach.h: FOG, NO SHAME, NO CARE, NO REST.
teach.b: Recklessness, anottappa: no care for what the act will do, to others or to oneself. And restlessness, uddhacca: the mind can't settle, like water stirred by wind. Here's something easy to miss.

teach.h: GREED AND ANGER: THEIR OWN FAMILIES.
teach.b: Greed and anger aren't on this list. They come and go, and the manual gives each its own family, coming over the next two days. These four sit underneath every unwholesome moment, a sharp word or a quiet bit of cruelty.
Restlessness may be the easiest of them to feel. On this account, an unwholesome moment is never fully at rest; there's a jitter in it. So nobody has to diagnose their own heart from the inside.

It's enough to feel for agitation, in the jaw, the hands, the speed of the next thought. Later this week, the manual shows the other side: two factors that are the exact opposites of shamelessness and recklessness.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the four unwholesome universals by their Pali names, and some meditation teachers in Theravada communities encourage students to notice restlessness as a sign that an unskillful state is present.

o: the four kinds of people the Buddha said to avoid
four factors under every unwholesome moment of mind
four sins that bring a person rebirth in hell

games.q: the troubled four: tap the pairs.

s: the four are greed, hatred, delusion and restlessness
greed and hatred have their own families. the four are delusion, shamelessness, recklessness and restlessness.
unwholesome is a verdict on the person
akusala means unskillful: a state that leads to harm. the Buddha's test for Rahula looks at the action, not the person.
the manual finds restlessness in every unwholesome moment
on this account, an unwholesome moment is never fully at rest.

games.q: you're building a house in rain country, with a thatched roof, and you're short on time. what do you do?
o: thatch it fast and patch the gaps later.
thatch it well, gap by gap.
skip the roof; it isn't raining yet.
games.why: the Dhammapada's verse: rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, and passion through an unreflecting mind. the gaps only show when the weather turns.

practice: If you'd like, let the breath come and go, then feel for any restlessness at all: a foot that wants to jiggle, a mind skipping to the next thing, a pull toward the phone.

Don't call it bad; just find where it lives, the hands, the chest, behind the eyes. Let one long breath out and see whether it settles a little or not; either way, it has been seen, and that is the whole practice.

wordCard.voice: The unwholesome four. Delusion, shamelessness, recklessness and restlessness: the four the manual finds in every unwholesome moment. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali uddhacca: restlessness, the mind that can't settle.
